metric.why: Transformer and switchgear lead times stretched from months to years and now gate construction schedules as hard as permits do. Lead-time surveys are published by industry groups and research firms; watch the directory sources.
metric.definition: Order-to-delivery time for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators.

reading.body:
Critical equipment lead times, not capital or permits alone, now set the pace at which data centers can be built.

The metric is order-to-delivery time for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators. The stated pattern is a stretch from months to years, which puts procurement on the construction schedule alongside permitting. The category places lead times next to hyperscaler and colocation capital expenditure and colocation rental rates, so equipment availability sits in the same accounting family as the money spent on the buildings and the revenue drawn from them.

This matters for AI because an accelerator is only useful once it is powered and cooled. A delayed transformer or cooling plant delays compute that has already been ordered and paid for. The binding constraint shifts from the chip to the electrical and mechanical plant around it, and a schedule slip in that plant is a slip in deliverable compute.

The data does not say how long any of these lead times currently are, which equipment is worst, or where. It defines the metric and notes that lead-time surveys are published by industry groups and research firms, so the figures live in those sources rather than here. A reader cannot tell from this whether lead times are still lengthening or have begun to ease.
